title: India Sends Eighth Aid Flight to Nepal as Flood Death Toll Tops 1,369
excerpt: With more than 130 tonnes of relief flown in across eight Air Force sorties and 54 specialists on the ground, India has mounted one of its largest humanitarian operations in flood-hit Nepal.
body:
• India has flown more than 130 tonnes of relief material to Nepal aboard eight Indian Air Force aircraft since August 26, with the eighth flight landing in Kathmandu on September 9 carrying 35 tonnes of supplies.
  • Fifty-four Indian specialists are on the ground: 30 tunnel rescue experts, 19 forensic experts and a five-member medical team, working with Nepalese authorities on search, rescue and victim identification.
  • Nepal's flash-flood death toll has climbed to 1,369, with 13,646 people rescued and 333 injured under treatment; an Indian tunnel rescue team is working with the Nepali Army at Chilime to reach trapped workers.
  • Some 275 Indian nationals remain unaccounted for in Nepal, while 166 have been rescued, according to the Ministry of External Affairs.

India has sharply intensified its humanitarian mission in Nepal, flying in more than 130 tonnes of relief material aboard eight Indian Air Force aircraft as the Himalayan nation's flash-flood death toll climbed to 1,369.

The eighth IAF aircraft, carrying 35 tonnes of essential relief and rescue supplies, landed in Kathmandu on Wednesday, marking the latest shipment in a continuous aid effort that began on August 26, according to the Ministry of External Affairs.

Eight flights and counting

The airlift has moved steadily from a rapid-response operation into a sustained relief campaign. At a briefing in New Delhi on September 4, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India had by then dispatched 95 tonnes of relief material across seven aircraft, with two planes alone flying 21 tonnes of supplies to Kathmandu in a single day.

Beyond standard relief supplies — temporary shelters, blankets, hygiene kits, solar lamps and essential medicines — India has shipped specialised technical equipment tailored to the disaster's most difficult challenges: mud rescue suits, gas detectors, breathing apparatus and inflatable walkways for tunnel and mud rescues, alongside portable generators, lighting towers and dewatering pumps. DNA kits, reagents and equipment for DNA profiling have also been sent to help identify victims.

Tunnel rescue at Chilime

The most dramatic front of the operation is unfolding underground. India's specialised tunnel rescue team began joint operations with the Nepali Army at two sites, Chilime and Langtang, and search efforts are now concentrated at the Chilime tunnel, where difficult terrain, restricted access and the tunnel's steep slope have slowed progress.

"The Indian tunnel rescue team has been persistent in its work and ensured good progress with manual efforts and the use of innovative techniques."

— Ministry of External Affairs, statement

To accelerate the operation, crews are building a makeshift path to bring heavy machinery, including an excavator, to the tunnel entrance. Construction of the track is progressing steadily and is expected to be completed within two to three days, the MEA said. India's forensic team, meanwhile, is working in two laboratories in Kathmandu alongside Nepalese experts to examine and analyse DNA samples, with more forensic laboratory equipment, DNA kits and reagents being supplied.

The toll on the ground

The scale of the disaster remains staggering. Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority reports 1,369 deaths, with the missing-persons figure revised after 102 identified bodies were deducted from the unaccounted list. A total of 13,646 people have been rescued so far.

Some 333 injured people are being treated at 19 hospitals, while 256 have been discharged. The Nepali Army has provided medical treatment to 3,535 people and the Armed Police Force to 3,606, underscoring the breadth of the domestic response India is now supplementing.

Indians caught in the floods

The disaster has hit close to home for India. As of last Friday, 275 Indian nationals remained unaccounted for in Nepal, while 166 had been rescued and 1,907 had safely crossed into Nepal from China. According to official sources in China, no Indian travellers are currently stranded in the Tibet Autonomous Region.

"Our rescue and forensic teams are deployed on the ground, and they are working closely with the Nepalese authorities."

— Randhir Jaiswal, MEA spokesperson

Jaiswal said India deeply appreciates the efforts of Nepal's authorities and confirmed that New Delhi plans to send additional forensic kits, Bailey bridges and other materials requested by the Nepalese government in the coming days.

What to watch

The operation is far from over. Excavator access at Chilime could change the tempo of the tunnel rescue within days, and the forensic identification effort in Kathmandu's laboratories will continue for weeks as DNA results come in. For the Indian diaspora, for whom Nepal is a familiar neighbour — thousands of Indians live, work and travel there, from Kailash-Mansarovar pilgrims to cross-border traders — the unfolding rescue is a reminder of how deeply the two countries' fortunes are intertwined. Further aid flights and equipment shipments are expected as Nepal's government submits new requests.
